hero.title: Understanding Lua
hero.description: A short, practical introduction to Lua — the language most FiveM scripts are written in. Below you can also write your own code and have it checked instantly.

sections.title: How Lua scripts work
sections.lead: Six building blocks that show up in almost every FiveM script.

items.title: Variables
items.description: `local` stores values your script remembers — names, numbers, or true/false flags.

items.title: Conditionals
items.description: `if / then / else / end` lets your script react differently depending on the situation.

items.title: Loops
items.description: `for ... do ... end` or `ipairs()` let you go through lists without writing out every entry by hand.

items.title: Tables
items.description: A table (`{}`) is Lua's central data structure — it can store lists and named fields at the same time.

items.title: Functions
items.description: A function bundles reusable logic under a name you can call anywhere in the script.

items.title: FiveM Events
items.description: `RegisterCommand` and `TriggerClientEvent` are how server and client scripts talk to each other.

frameworksTeaser.title: ESX, QBCore or Qbox?
frameworksTeaser.lead: A short overview of how the three major FiveM frameworks work and differ.

hero.title: ESX, QBCore & Qbox
hero.description: A framework gives a FiveM server its core systems — jobs, inventory, banking and more — so every script doesn't start from zero. I develop for all three major frameworks equally.

intro.title: What a framework handles
intro.lead: Nearly every framework ships these core systems — scripts build on top of them instead of reinventing them.

cards.title: The three big options
cards.lead: Each framework has a different maturity level and target audience.

items.name: ESX
items.description: The historical market leader with the largest script catalog around and very beginner-friendly. New feature development has, however, largely stalled.
items.bestFor: Best for: existing ESX servers that don't need a full rebuild.

items.name: QBCore
items.description: The modern standard since 2020, with cleaner code and better performance than ESX, plus a huge ecosystem of free and premium scripts. Active development has also largely stalled here.
items.bestFor: Best for: servers built on the large existing QBCore script ecosystem.

items.name: Qbox
items.description: A community fork of QBCore that pushes modularity and modern Lua practices further (including ox_lib), while staying largely backwards compatible with existing QBCore resources.
items.bestFor: Best for: new servers in 2026 that want an actively maintained foundation.

rows.name: QBCore
rows.ecosystem: Very large, lots of premium content

frameworks.positioning: Whether your server already runs on ESX or QBCore, or you want to start fresh with Qbox in 2026 — I build scripts and customizations for all three frameworks.

hero.title: Set up your own server
hero.description: Spinning up your own FiveM server is quicker than most people think. This guide takes you from downloading the server artifacts to your first launch – for both Windows and Linux, including the pitfalls beginners typically fall into.

requirements.title: What you need
requirements.lead: Whether Windows or Linux – you can't get going without these four things.

items.label: Hardware
items.detail: A machine or VPS with at least 4 GB of RAM and a modern CPU. Your own PC is fine for testing; for 24/7 operation rent a dedicated or virtual server.

items.label: Cfx.re account
items.detail: A free account on portal.cfx.re. That's where you create the license key the server won't start without.

items.label: Git
items.detail: To clone the server-data base resources. On Windows from git-scm.com, on Linux via your package manager.

items.label: Open port
items.detail: Port 30120 (TCP and UDP) must be opened in your firewall and router so other players can connect.

setup.title: From download to a running server
setup.lead: Five steps to your first launch. Switch between Windows and Linux – the commands adapt.
setup.note: Note: Cfx.re provides the Linux version only as a "courtesy port" – bug fixes land on Windows first. For getting started, Windows is usually the smoother path.

windows.title: Download the artifacts
windows.body: Grab the current build marked "recommended" from the Server Download page and extract it with 7-Zip or WinRAR into C:\FXServer\server. Never take the very latest build – it can be unstable.

windows.title: Clone server-data
windows.body: The base resources (chat, spawnmanager, mapmanager …) live in a Git repo. Clone them into a separate folder next to the artifacts.

windows.title: Create a license key
windows.body: Sign in at portal.cfx.re and create a free server key. You'll put it into server.cfg next – and never push it to a public repo.

windows.title: Create server.cfg
windows.body: server.cfg is the heart of your server: ports, name, slots, license and which resources start. Create it in the server-data folder.

windows.title: Start the server
windows.body: Switch into the server-data folder and start FXServer.exe with your config. txAdmin runs automatically – open localhost:40120 in the browser to manage the server from a UI.

linux.title: Install packages & artifacts
linux.body: Install Git and xz-utils, create the folder structure and extract the downloaded Linux build (fx.tar.xz).

linux.title: Clone server-data
linux.body: Clone the base resources into a separate folder next to the server binaries.

linux.title: Create a license key
linux.body: Create a free key at portal.cfx.re. It goes into server.cfg and never belongs in a public repo.

linux.title: Create server.cfg
linux.body: Ports, name, slots, license and startup resources – all of it goes into server.cfg in the server-data folder.

linux.title: Start the server
linux.body: Start the server via run.sh. For 24/7 operation wrap it in a screen or tmux session (or a systemd service) so it keeps running after you log out.

snippets.linuxDownload: # download fx.tar.xz from the Server Download page, then:

items.title: Always the "recommended" build
items.body: The newest artifact build is often bleeding edge. For a stable server pick the one marked green as "recommended".

items.title: The license key is secret
items.body: Never push sv_licenseKey to a public GitHub repo. If the key leaks, you can revoke it on portal.cfx.re and create a new one.

items.title: Open port 30120
items.body: If nobody can connect from outside, it's almost always the missing forward in the router (port forwarding) and firewall – for both TCP and UDP.

items.title: Use txAdmin
items.body: Instead of configuring everything by hand, txAdmin (port 40120) walks you through setup, deployment and management in a UI. The easiest path for beginners.

items.title: OneSync for more than 32 slots
items.body: If you want more than 32 players at once, you need OneSync – enabled via the server configuration in the Cfx portal.

server.outro: Once your server is running, it's time for the frameworks: ESX, QBCore or Qbox provide the base systems your scripts build on.
